chapter_note.about: Linear discriminant analysis finds a direction on which labelled classes look as separate as possible. It scores a direction by how far apart the class means land, divided by how spread out each class lands. This chapter builds the two scatter matrices, the Fisher score, the closed-form direction for two classes, the eigenproblem and its rank limit, how to cut on the projected line, the link to a Gaussian classifier, and the difference from PCA.

chapter_note.simple: LDA is a way to look at labelled data from the best angle. It looks for a line on which the group averages are far apart and each group is bunched up tight. Every point becomes a single number on that line, and a cut-off between the group averages decides the class. With two groups the best line has a ready formula. With more groups you get at most one line fewer than the number of groups. PCA only cares about spread, but LDA also reads the labels, so it can pick a line where the data looks narrow but the groups differ.

cards.title: Class means and scatter matrices
cards.simple: Picture two groups of students scattered across a playground. First find the centre of each group, its average position. Then measure how spread out each group is around its own centre. That is the 'within-class scatter'. Separately, note how far apart the two centres are. That is the 'between-class scatter'. LDA will later look for a view where the gap is big and the spreads are small. In exam words: $S_W=\sum_c\sum_{x\in c}(x-\mu_c)(x-\mu_c)^\top$, and for two classes $S_B=(\mu_1-\mu_2)(\mu_1-\mu_2)^\top$.
cards.idea: LDA starts with two kinds of spread. The **within-class scatter** $S_W$ measures how far points sit from the mean of their **own** class. The **between-class scatter** $S_B$ measures how far the class means sit from each other. You want the second big and the first small.
cards.definition:
$$\mu_c=\frac1{n_c}\sum_{x\in c}x,\qquad S_W=\sum_c\sum_{x\in c}(x-\mu_c)(x-\mu_c)^\top,\qquad S_B=(\mu_1-\mu_2)(\mu_1-\mu_2)^\top$$

Symbols: $\mu_c$ is the mean of class $c$ and $n_c$ its number of points. $(x-\mu_c)(x-\mu_c)^\top$ is a column times a row, which gives a square matrix. For $C$ classes, $S_B=\sum_c n_c(\mu_c-\mu)(\mu_c-\mu)^\top$ with $\mu$ the mean of all points.
cards.intuition_full: In one dimension, spread is one number: add up the squared distances from the mean. In two or more dimensions the spread has a shape, because a cloud can be long in one direction and thin in another. The scatter matrix keeps that shape. Its diagonal holds the spread along each axis. Its off-diagonal entries record whether the two coordinates grow together. To build it, take each point's offset from its class mean, multiply the offset column by its own row, and add up the small matrices. Offsets are measured from the class's own mean, so $S_W$ ignores where the classes sit and keeps only the shape of each cloud. $S_B$ is the opposite: it ignores shape and keeps only the gap between the means. For two classes $S_B$ is one column times one row, so it points in one direction only. Using the global mean inside $S_W$ is the usual slip, because it mixes the gap into the spread.

examples.setup: Class 1 has the points $(1,2),(2,4),(3,3)$. Class 2 has $(6,5),(7,7),(8,6)$. Find both class means, the within-class scatter $S_W$ and the between-class scatter $S_B$.
steps: Six points in two clouds. Class 1 sits lower left and class 2 upper right.

Class 1 offsets from $(2,3)$: $(-1,-1),(0,1),(1,0)$. Outer products: $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}=S_1$.
Class 2 offsets from $(7,6)$ are the same three offsets, so $S_2=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$.
$S_W=S_1+S_2=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$. With $d=\mu_1-\mu_2=(-5,-3)$, $S_B=dd^\top=\begin{pmatrix}25&15\\15&9\end{pmatrix}$.
examples.answer: $\mu_1=(2,3)$, $\mu_2=(7,6)$, $S_W=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$, $S_B=\begin{pmatrix}25&15\\15&9\end{pmatrix}$.

steps: Class means $\mu_1=3$ and $\mu_2=10$. Overall mean $\mu=36/5=7.2$.
Trap: measuring every point from the global mean 7.2 gives 68.8. That is the total, not the within-class part.
examples.answer: $S_W=10$, $S_B=58.8$, $S_T=68.8$. Use each class's own mean for $S_W$.

examples.setup: Is the two-class $S_B=\begin{pmatrix}25&15\\15&9\end{pmatrix}$ from the basic example invertible?
steps: Both rows are multiples of $d=(5,3)$ (the second is $0.6$ times the first), because $S_B$ is one column times one row.
A zero determinant means no inverse. $S_B$ has rank 1.
examples.answer: $S_B$ is singular with rank 1. Only $S_W$ is ever inverted in LDA.

cards.why: $S_W$ and $S_B$ are the two building blocks of LDA. The Fisher score, the eigen-equation and the direction formula are all written with them. In GATE: the LDA items assume you know what they mean, and ladder questions ask you to compute them from a few points.
how: Find the **mean** of each class (average every coordinate).
Subtract the class mean from each point of that class.
Multiply each offset (a column) by its own transpose (a row) and add up over the class.
Add the class matrices to get $S_W$. For two classes, $S_B$ is the outer product of the mean difference with itself.
cards.mistake: Using the global mean instead of the class mean when building $S_W$. That adds the gap between classes into the spread and returns the total scatter. Subtract each point's own class mean.
edge_cases: A class with one point has zero scatter, because the point is its own mean.
$S_W$ is symmetric: its two off-diagonal entries are equal.
$S_B=dd^\top$ for two classes always has rank 1.
Some books divide by $n$ to get a covariance. Use the definition the question gives.

cards.title: Fisher criterion
cards.simple: Suppose you look at the playground from one side so that the two groups look as far apart as possible. From some angles the groups overlap, and from others they sit apart. Score each angle by two things: how far apart the group centres look, and how smeared out each group looks. A good angle has far-apart centres and tight groups. The score is the gap squared divided by the smear. Only the angle matters, not how long you draw the line. In exam words: $J(w)=\dfrac{w^\top S_Bw}{w^\top S_Ww}$, and $J(cw)=J(w)$.
cards.idea: Fisher's idea is to squash the data onto a line with direction $w$ and score the line. The score $J(w)$ is the **squared gap** between the projected class means divided by the **total projected spread** of the classes. A big $J$ means the classes sit far apart and are tight. LDA picks the $w$ with the biggest $J$. Stretching $w$ changes nothing, so only its direction matters.
cards.definition:
$$J(w)=\frac{(m_1-m_2)^2}{s_1^2+s_2^2}=\frac{w^\top S_B\,w}{w^\top S_W\,w}$$

Symbols: $m_c=w^\top\mu_c$ is the projected mean of class $c$. $s_c^2=\sum_{x\in c}(w^\top x-m_c)^2$ is its projected scatter. $S_B$ and $S_W$ are the matrices from the last card.
cards.intuition_full: Projecting means turning every point $x$ into one number $z=w^\top x$, its shadow along $w$. The shadows of class 1 have a mean $m_1$ and a scatter $s_1^2$. Those of class 2 have $m_2$ and $s_2^2$. The top of $J$ rewards a big gap between the means, squared so the sign does not matter. The bottom punishes spread: if each class is smeared, the shadows overlap even when the means are apart. So $J$ works like a signal-to-noise ratio. The matrix form comes from algebra: $(w^\top\mu_1-w^\top\mu_2)^2=w^\top(\mu_1-\mu_2)(\mu_1-\mu_2)^\top w=w^\top S_Bw$, and the two projected scatters add up to $w^\top S_Ww$. Doubling $w$ doubles every shadow. The gap squared grows 4 times and the spread grows 4 times, so $J$ stays put. That is why any scalar multiple of the best $w$ is also best.

examples.setup: Use the points of the last card: class 1 $(1,2),(2,4),(3,3)$ and class 2 $(6,5),(7,7),(8,6)$. Find $J$ for the directions $w=(1,0)$, $w=(0,1)$ and $w=(1,1)$. Then see what happens when $w$ is doubled.
steps: Each direction turns the six points into six numbers. We score each set of numbers.
$w=(1,0)$: class 1 gives $1,2,3$ (mean 2, scatter 2). Class 2 gives $6,7,8$ (mean 7, scatter 2). $J=(7-2)^2/(2+2)=25/4=6.25$.
$w=(0,1)$: class 1 gives $2,4,3$ (mean 3, scatter 2). Class 2 gives $5,7,6$ (mean 6, scatter 2). $J=3^2/4=2.25$.
$w=(1,1)$: class 1 gives $3,6,6$ (mean 5, scatter 6). Class 2 gives $11,14,14$ (mean 13, scatter 6). $J=8^2/12=5.33$. The gap is bigger here, but the spread is much bigger too.
Of the three, the $x$-axis wins. Double it, $w=(2,0)$: class 1 gives $2,4,6$ and class 2 gives $12,14,16$. $J=10^2/(8+8)=6.25$, unchanged.

examples.setup: $S_B=dd^\top$ with $d=(3,1)$, and $S_W=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$. Which gives the larger $J$: $w=(1,0)$ or $w=(1,1)$? Also find $J$ for $w=(2,2)$.
steps: Since $S_B=dd^\top$, $w^\top S_Bw=(w\cdot d)^2$.
$w=(1,0)$: $w\cdot d=3$, so the top is $9$. $w^\top S_Ww=1$. $J=9/1=9$.
$w=(1,1)$: $w\cdot d=4$, so the top is $16$. $w^\top S_Ww=1\cdot1+1\cdot2=3$. $J=16/3=5.33$.
examples.answer: $w=(1,0)$ is better, $9>5.33$. $J(2,2)=J(1,1)=5.33$ because scaling does not matter.

examples.setup: Same matrices. Find $J$ for $w=(1,-3)$, a direction perpendicular to $d=(3,1)$.
steps: $w\cdot d=3-3=0$, so $w^\top S_Bw=0$.
$w^\top S_Ww=1\cdot1+2\cdot9=19>0$.
examples.answer: $J=0$. If the projected means coincide, no amount of tightness helps.

cards.why: $J$ is the quantity LDA maximises. Everything else in the chapter, the direction formula and the eigen-equation, comes from maximising it. In GATE: the equation satisfied by the maximiser (2024), and ladder questions that evaluate $J$ for a given $w$.
how: Project: compute $w^\top x$ for every point, or use $w^\top S_Bw$ and $w^\top S_Ww$ directly.
Find the projected class means and the projected scatters.
Divide the squared gap of the means by the sum of the scatters.
Remember that $w$ and $cw$ give the same $J$.
cards.mistake: Thinking a longer $w$ is better, or that $J$ rewards the gap alone. Length cancels in the ratio. And a big gap can come with big spread: the diagonal in the example has the largest gap (8) but a lower $J$ than the $x$-axis because its spread is three times larger.
edge_cases: $J(w)=J(cw)$ for any $c\ne0$, including negative $c$.
$J\ge0$ always: a square over a sum of squares.
$J=0$ when $w$ is perpendicular to the mean difference.
$w=0$ is not allowed, since both top and bottom are 0.

cards.title: Two-class Fisher direction
cards.simple: Is there a shortcut to the best angle? For two groups there is. Start with the line joining the two group centres. Then bend it away from the directions where the groups are naturally spread out. The bending is done by multiplying with the inverse of the within-group spread matrix. Directions where the groups are very spread get less weight, and directions where they are tight get more. In exam words: $w\propto S_W^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2)$ and $J_{\max}=d^\top S_W^{-1}d$.
cards.idea: For two classes the best direction has a formula. Start from the **mean difference** $d=\mu_1-\mu_2$ and multiply it by $S_W^{-1}$. If $S_W$ is a multiple of the identity, $w$ is just $d$. Otherwise the inverse tilts $w$ away from the directions in which the classes are naturally spread.
cards.definition:
$$w\ \propto\ S_W^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2),\qquad J_{\max}=d^\top S_W^{-1}d,\qquad d=\mu_1-\mu_2$$

Symbols: $S_W^{-1}$ is the inverse of the within-class scatter. $\propto$ means 'equal up to a scale factor', so length and sign do not matter. For a $2\times2$ matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&e\end{pmatrix}$ the inverse is $\frac1{ae-bc}\begin{pmatrix}e&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}$.
cards.intuition_full: Why the inverse? Think of $S_W$ as the shape of the classes. If the clouds are long along some direction, moving along it does not tell the classes apart, because points of one class are spread out there anyway. A good $w$ should avoid long directions. $S_W^{-1}$ has big entries exactly where $S_W$ has small ones, so it shrinks long directions and stretches tight ones. Another way to see it: first stretch the data until each cloud looks round. Now every direction is equally spread, so the best line is just the line between the means. Undoing the stretch gives $S_W^{-1}d$. In the example the clouds are long along $(1,1)$ and the mean difference $d=(5,3)$ leans partly along that long direction. The inverse tilts it to $(7,1)$, which is closer to the tight direction $(1,-1)$.

examples.setup: Use the data of the last cards: $S_W=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$ and means $(2,3)$ and $(7,6)$. Find the Fisher direction, and compare $J$ along it with $J$ along the plain mean difference.
steps: Mean difference $d=\mu_2-\mu_1=(5,3)$. The clouds are long along $(1,1)$.
$\det S_W=4\cdot4-2\cdot2=12$. So $S_W^{-1}=\frac1{12}\begin{pmatrix}4&-2\\-2&4\end{pmatrix}$.
examples.answer: $w\propto(7,1)$ with $J=6.33$, better than the plain mean difference with $J=5.90$.

examples.setup: Two classes have $S_W=\begin{pmatrix}5&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix}$ and mean difference $d=(1,3)$. Find the ratio $w_2/w_1$ of the Fisher direction and the maximum value of $J$.
steps: $\det S_W=5\cdot2-2\cdot2=6$. $S_W^{-1}=\frac16\begin{pmatrix}2&-2\\-2&5\end{pmatrix}$.
$J_{\max}=d^\top S_W^{-1}d=\frac16\bigl(1\cdot(-4)+3\cdot13\bigr)=35/6=5.83$.

examples.setup: $S_W=3I$ and $d=(2,-4)$. What is the Fisher direction?

cards.title: Generalised eigenproblem and rank
cards.simple: Sometimes you want not just the best angle but a ranked list of good ones. Each good angle comes with a score, called an eigenvalue, which is the value $J$ takes at that angle. For two groups there is exactly one useful angle, because the gap between two centres is a single line. Three groups give at most two, four groups at most three, and so on. The extra angles all score zero. In exam words: $S_Bw=\lambda S_Ww$, or $S_W^{-1}S_Bw=\lambda w$, and at most $\min(d,C-1)$ eigenvalues are non-zero.
cards.idea: At the best $w$ the slope of $J$ is zero. That gives the **generalised eigenproblem** $S_Bw=\lambda S_Ww$. Multiply by $S_W^{-1}$ to get an ordinary one, $S_W^{-1}S_Bw=\lambda w$. The eigenvalue $\lambda$ equals $J$ at that $w$, so the biggest eigenvalue gives the best direction. $S_B$ has rank at most $C-1$, so at most $\min(d,C-1)$ eigenvalues are non-zero.
cards.definition:
$$S_Bw=\lambda S_Ww\iff S_W^{-1}S_Bw=\lambda w,\qquad \#\{\lambda\ne0\}\le\min(d,\ C-1)$$

Symbols: $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue and $w$ its eigenvector. $d$ is the number of features and $C$ the number of classes. The eigenvalue is the value of $J$: $\lambda=\dfrac{w^\top S_Bw}{w^\top S_Ww}$.
cards.intuition_full: At the best direction $J$ cannot be improved by turning $w$ a little, so its slope is zero there. Working out that slope for the ratio gives $S_Bw\,(w^\top S_Ww)=S_Ww\,(w^\top S_Bw)$. Divide both sides by $w^\top S_Ww$ and call $\lambda=\frac{w^\top S_Bw}{w^\top S_Ww}$, which is $J$ itself. The result is $S_Bw=\lambda S_Ww$. So every stationary direction is an eigenvector, and its eigenvalue is its own score. The rank rule has a simple source. $S_B$ is built from the $C$ class means. Measured from the overall mean they satisfy one linear relation (their weighted sum is zero), so they span at most $C-1$ directions. A matrix built from $C-1$ independent directions has rank at most $C-1$. So $S_W^{-1}S_B$ has at most $C-1$ non-zero eigenvalues, and never more than $d$.

examples.setup: For the running data, $S_B=\begin{pmatrix}25&15\\15&9\end{pmatrix}$ and $S_W^{-1}=\frac1{12}\begin{pmatrix}4&-2\\-2&4\end{pmatrix}$. Find the eigenvalues of $M=S_W^{-1}S_B$ and the eigenvector of the larger one.
steps: $S_B$ has rank 1: its second row is $0.6$ times its first ($15/25=9/15$).

$M=\frac1{12}\begin{pmatrix}4\cdot25-2\cdot15&4\cdot15-2\cdot9\\-2\cdot25+4\cdot15&-2\cdot15+4\cdot9\end{pmatrix}=\frac1{12}\begin{pmatrix}70&42\\10&6\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}35/6&7/2\\5/6&1/2\end{pmatrix}$.
Trace $=35/6+1/2=19/3$. Determinant $=\frac{35}{6}\cdot\frac12-\frac72\cdot\frac56=\frac{35}{12}-\frac{35}{12}=0$. So $\lambda^2-\frac{19}3\lambda=0$, giving $\lambda=19/3=6.33$ and $\lambda=0$.
For $\lambda=19/3$: $(35/6-19/3)u_1+\frac72u_2=-\frac12u_1+\frac72u_2=0$, so $u_1=7u_2$ and $u\propto(7,1)$. That is the Fisher direction. Only one eigenvalue is non-zero, as $C-1=1$.
examples.answer: Eigenvalues $19/3\approx6.33$ and $0$. The eigenvector for $6.33$ is $(7,1)$, which matches the last card.

cards.title: Projection and threshold
cards.simple: After picking the best angle, every point becomes a single number: its shadow on that line. Now the job is easy. Put one marker on the line between the two piles of shadows. A new point goes to the pile on its side of the marker. If both groups are equally common and equally spread, the marker sits exactly halfway between the two group averages. In exam words: the score is $z=w^\top x$. With equal priors and equal projected spread the threshold is the midpoint of the projected means. The scale of $w$ does not matter.
cards.idea: Once you have $w$, turn each point into one number, $z=w^\top x$, its shadow on the line. Find the mean of $z$ for each class. With equal priors and equal spread, put the **threshold at the midpoint** of the two projected means. A new point goes to the class on its side of the threshold.
cards.definition:
$$z=w^\top x,\qquad t=\frac{w^\top\mu_1+w^\top\mu_2}{2}=w^\top\,\frac{\mu_1+\mu_2}{2}$$

Symbols: $z$ is the projected score, $t$ the threshold, $\mu_c$ the class means. A new point is assigned to the class whose projected mean lies on its side of $t$.
cards.intuition_full: A dot product $w^\top x$ adds up each coordinate times its weight. It is one number that measures how far $x$ lies along $w$ (scaled by the length of $w$). Projection is linear, so the projected mean of a class is the projection of its mean. That is why the threshold can be found two ways: project every point and average, or project the two means directly. The midpoint has a clear reason. If the shadows of both classes are bell-shaped with the same spread and the classes are equally likely, the two bells cross exactly halfway between their centres. Scaling $w$ by 2 doubles every shadow and the threshold, so decisions do not change. Flipping the sign of $w$ mirrors the line. Now the class that was on the right is on the left, but each point still lands on its own class's side.

examples.setup: Use $w=(7,1)$ from the last cards, with class 1 $(1,2),(2,4),(3,3)$ and class 2 $(6,5),(7,7),(8,6)$. Project the points, find the threshold, and classify the new point $(5,4)$.
steps: Threshold $t=(17+55)/2=36$, with equal priors and equal spread.
$39>36$, and 39 is 16 from 55 but 22 from 17. Predict class 2.
examples.answer: Threshold $36$. The point $(5,4)$ has score $39$ and goes to class 2.

New point: $z=0.8\cdot5+0.6\cdot5=7.0$.

cards.title: LDA as a Gaussian classifier
cards.simple: Now picture each group as a cloud with the same shape but a different centre. The classifier asks which cloud would most likely have produced this point. If both clouds have the same shape and size, the answer is a straight dividing line halfway between the centres. If one group is more common, slide the line a little toward the rarer group, so the common group gets more room. If the clouds are round, the straight line is simply 'closest centre wins'. In exam words: Gaussian classes with a shared covariance $\Sigma$ give a linear boundary $w^\top x+b=0$ with $w=\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2)$. With $\Sigma=\sigma^2I$ it becomes the nearest-centroid rule.
cards.idea: LDA can also classify. Assume each class is Gaussian with **the same covariance** $\Sigma$ and a different mean. Then the best (Bayes) decision boundary is a **straight line**, or a flat plane in higher dimensions. With equal priors it passes through the midpoint of the means. Unequal priors slide it toward the rarer class. If $\Sigma=\sigma^2I$ (round clouds) the rule is just 'nearest class mean'.
cards.definition:
$$w=\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2),\qquad \text{class 1 if } w^\top x+b>0,\quad b=-\tfrac12\,w^\top(\mu_1+\mu_2)+\ln\frac{P_1}{P_2}$$

Symbols: $\Sigma$ is the shared covariance and $P_1,P_2$ are the priors. In one dimension with variance $\sigma^2$ the boundary is at $x^*=\dfrac{\mu_1+\mu_2}{2}+\dfrac{\sigma^2}{\mu_1-\mu_2}\ln\dfrac{P_2}{P_1}$.
cards.intuition_full: Class 1 is more likely at $x$ when $P_1f_1(x)>P_2f_2(x)$, where $f_c$ is the density. Take logs. For a Gaussian the log-density is $-\tfrac12(x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)$ plus a constant. When $\Sigma$ is the same for both classes, the quadratic piece $x^\top\Sigma^{-1}x$ shows up on both sides and cancels. What is left is linear in $x$. If the covariances differ, the quadratic pieces do not cancel and the boundary curves (that method is called QDA). The prior adds the constant $\ln(P_1/P_2)$: the more common class gets a head start and its region grows. In one dimension this is the crossing point of the two prior-weighted bell curves sliding sideways. For round clouds $\Sigma^{-1}$ is a multiple of the identity, so $w\propto\mu_1-\mu_2$ and the boundary is the perpendicular bisector of the segment between the means.

examples.setup: One feature. Class 1 is Gaussian with mean 1 and class 2 with mean 5. Both have variance $\sigma^2=2$. Find the boundary when priors are equal, then when $P_1=0.7$ and $P_2=0.3$.
steps: Equal priors: the weighted curves are mirror images, so they cross at the midpoint $(1+5)/2=3$.
Priors $0.7$ and $0.3$: multiply each density by its prior. The class-1 curve grows and the class-2 curve shrinks, so the crossing moves.
Shift $=-0.5\times(-0.847)=+0.424$. The boundary is $3+0.424=3.424$, moved toward the rarer class 2.
examples.answer: Boundary $3$ for equal priors and $3.424$ for priors $0.7/0.3$.

examples.setup: A nearest-centroid classifier has means $\mu_r=(2,0)$ and $\mu_g=(0,4)$. Show that its boundary is a line, and classify $x=(1,3)$.
steps: The difference is $f(x)=\|x-\mu_r\|^2-\|x-\mu_g\|^2=-4x_1+8x_2-12$. The squared terms cancel, so it is linear.
The boundary $f=0$ is $-x_1+2x_2=3$, a straight line.
At $x=(1,3)$: $f=-4+24-12=8>0$, so $x$ is farther from $\mu_r$. Distances: $\|x-\mu_r\|^2=10$ and $\|x-\mu_g\|^2=2$. Class g.
examples.answer: The boundary is the line $-x_1+2x_2=3$. The point $(1,3)$ goes to class g.

examples.setup: Two classes share the mean 0 and have equal priors, but variances 1 and 4. Where do the posteriors tie?
steps: Set $\dfrac1{1}e^{-x^2/2}=\dfrac1{2}e^{-x^2/8}$. Take logs: $-\dfrac{x^2}2+\dfrac{x^2}8=-\ln2$.
Class 1 wins inside $|x|<1.36$ and class 2 wins on both outer sides.
examples.answer: Two boundary points, $\pm1.36$. With unequal covariances the boundary is not linear.

how: Check that the classes share a covariance $\Sigma$.

cards.title: LDA versus PCA
cards.simple: Both PCA and LDA squash many measurements into fewer. PCA never looks at the labels. It keeps the direction where the data is spread out the most, like photographing a crowd from the angle where it looks widest. LDA does look at the labels. It keeps the direction where the groups look most different, even if the crowd looks narrow from that side. Sometimes the widest view is useless for telling the groups apart. So PCA is for compressing and LDA is for separating. In exam words: PCA is unsupervised and maximises variance. LDA is supervised and maximises $J$. LDA gives at most $C-1$ directions.
cards.idea: **PCA** takes the direction of largest total variance and never reads the labels. **LDA** takes the direction that best separates the labelled classes. When the classes differ along a direction with small spread, PCA throws away exactly what LDA keeps. PCA can give up to $d$ directions, while LDA gives at most $C-1$.
cards.definition:
$$\text{PCA: }\max_{\|u\|=1}\ u^\top S_Tu\qquad\text{LDA: }\max_w\ \frac{w^\top S_Bw}{w^\top S_Ww}$$

Symbols: $S_T$ is the total scatter of all points around the overall mean (with the weighted $S_B$, $S_T=S_W+S_B$). PCA uses only $S_T$, so labels play no part.
cards.intuition_full: Think of a photo of two groups of runners taken from the side. The runners are spread out along the track, but the track is long for both groups. PCA says the biggest variation is along the track, so it keeps that direction. If one group is simply taller, the useful difference is height, a direction with small variance. LDA divides the gap by the spread, so a tight direction with a real gap beats a loose direction with no gap. The example shows this: $x$ has a huge spread but is the same for both classes, while $y$ has a small spread but separates them. PCA picks $x$ and lays both classes on top of each other. The limits also differ. PCA can give up to $d$ components (at most $n-1$ non-zero ones when there are $n$ samples). LDA is limited by the number of classes, at most $C-1$. When the classes are separated along the direction of largest spread, both pick the same line.

examples.setup: Class 1: $(-4,1),(-4,3),(4,1),(4,3)$. Class 2: $(-4,5),(-4,7),(4,5),(4,7)$. Find the PCA direction and the LDA direction, and the Fisher score of each.
steps: The $x$ values are $\pm4$ for both classes. The $y$ values are $1,3$ for class 1 and $5,7$ for class 2.
Total scatter: along $x$, $\sum x^2=8\cdot16=128$. Along $y$ (mean 4), $\sum(y-4)^2=40$. PCA picks the largest, the $x$-axis.
Project onto $x$: class 1 gives $-4,-4,4,4$ and class 2 gives $-4,-4,4,4$. The means are 0 and 0, so $J=0$. The classes sit on top of each other.
LDA: each class has $S=\operatorname{diag}(64,4)$, so $S_W=\operatorname{diag}(128,8)$. Means $(0,2)$ and $(0,6)$, so $d=(0,4)$. $w\propto S_W^{-1}d=(0,\tfrac48)\propto(0,1)$, the $y$-axis.
Project onto $y$: class 1 gives $1,3,1,3$ (mean 2, scatter 4). Class 2 gives $5,7,5,7$ (mean 6, scatter 4). $J=(6-2)^2/(4+4)=2$, and a cut at $y=4$ separates them perfectly.
examples.answer: PCA picks the $x$-axis ($J=0$, classes overlap). LDA picks the $y$-axis ($J=2$, perfectly separated).

examples.setup: A dataset has $d=10$ features, $n=6$ samples and $C=3$ classes. What are the maximum numbers of non-zero PCA components and LDA directions? What happens to each if the class labels are shuffled?
steps: PCA centres the data. Six centred points span at most $n-1=5$ directions, so at most $\min(10,5)=5$ non-zero components.
LDA: $S_B$ is built from 3 class means and has rank at most $C-1=2$. So at most $\min(10,2)=2$ directions.
Shuffle the labels: the points do not move, so the PCA components stay the same.
But the class means, $S_B$ and $S_W$ change, so the LDA directions change.
examples.answer: PCA $\le5$ and LDA $\le2$. Shuffling labels changes LDA only.

steps: Total scatter: $x$ values give $\sum x^2=136$ (the mean is 0), and $y$ gives $\sum(y-2)^2=8$. PCA picks the $x$-axis.
Means $(-4,2)$ and $(4,2)$, so $d=(-8,0)$. Each class has $S=\operatorname{diag}(4,4)$, so $S_W=\operatorname{diag}(8,8)$.
$w\propto S_W^{-1}d\propto(1,0)$, also the $x$-axis.
examples.answer: Both pick the $x$-axis. When the classes separate along the direction of largest spread, PCA and LDA agree.

scenes.title: Class means and the two scatter matrices

steps.caption: Two classes of three points each. Class 1 sits lower left, class 2 upper right.
Class 1 offsets from (2, 3): (−1,−1), (0,1), (1,0). Each offset times its own transpose gives a small matrix. They add up to S1 = [[2,1],[1,2]].
Class 2 offsets from (7, 6) are the same three, so S2 = [[2,1],[1,2]] as well.
S_W = S1 + S2 = [[4,2],[2,4]]. The gap between the means d = (−5, −3) gives S_B = d d^T = [[25,15],[15,9]].

scenes.title: Score each direction by gap squared over spread

steps.caption: Six points in two classes. We look for a direction w that pushes the class means apart while keeping each class tight.
w = (1, 0): shadows on the x-axis. Class 1 gives 1, 2, 3 (mean 2, scatter 2). Class 2 gives 6, 7, 8 (mean 7, scatter 2). J = 5² / 4 = 6.25.
w = (0, 1): shadows on the y-axis. Class 1 gives 2, 4, 3 (mean 3). Class 2 gives 5, 7, 6 (mean 6). The means are closer: J = 3² / 4 = 2.25.
w = (1, 1): the diagonal. Class 1 gives 3, 6, 6 (mean 5, scatter 6). Class 2 gives 11, 14, 14 (mean 13, scatter 6). The gap is 8 but the spread is 12: J = 64/12 = 5.33.
Of the three, the x-axis wins. Now stretch it to w = (2, 0): every shadow doubles (2, 4, 6 and 12, 14, 16), but J = 10² / 16 = 6.25 is unchanged.

scenes.title: S_W inverse tilts the mean difference into the Fisher direction

objects.text: J along d: 5.90,  J along w: 6.33

steps.caption: Class means (2, 3) and (7, 6). The mean difference d = μ2 − μ1 = (5, 3) points straight from one cloud to the other.
The clouds are long along (1, 1). S_W = [[4,2],[2,4]] has determinant 4·4 − 2·2 = 12, so S_W^-1 = (1/12)[[4,−2],[−2,4]].
Multiply: S_W^-1 d = (1/12)(4·5 − 2·3, −2·5 + 4·3) = (1/12)(14, 2), which points along (7, 1). The arrow tilts away from the long diagonal.
Compare scores: J along d is 34²/196 = 5.90, J along w is 38²/228 = 6.33. The tilted direction separates better.

scenes.title: Eigenvalues of S_W inverse times S_B

steps.caption: S_B = d d^T for the running data. Its second row is 0.6 times the first, so it has rank 1.
Trace 19/3 and determinant 0 give λ² − (19/3)λ = 0, so λ = 19/3 ≈ 6.33 and λ = 0. Only one eigenvalue is non-zero, since C − 1 = 1.
For λ = 19/3 the first row gives −u1/2 + 7u2/2 = 0, so u1 = 7u2 and u ∝ (7, 1). This is the Fisher direction from the last card.

scenes.title: Project to scores, cut at the midpoint of the class means

steps.caption: Project every point with z = 7x1 + x2. Class 1 scores: 9, 18, 24. Class 2 scores: 47, 56, 62. Each point is now one number on a line.
Projected class means: (9 + 18 + 24)/3 = 17 and (47 + 56 + 62)/3 = 55.
With equal priors and equal spread, the threshold is the midpoint (17 + 55)/2 = 36.
A new point (5, 4) has score z = 7·5 + 4 = 39. It lands just right of the threshold.
39 > 36, and 39 is 16 from 55 but 22 from 17. Predict class 2.

scenes.title: Priors slide the boundary toward the rarer class

steps.caption: Two Gaussian classes with the same variance 2, means 1 and 5. With equal priors the two curves are mirror images and cross halfway, at x = 3.

The crossing moves by σ² / (μ1 − μ2) × ln(P2/P1). Here ln(0.3/0.7) = ln 0.4286 = −0.847.
Shift = (2 / −4) × (−0.847) = +0.424. The boundary moves to 3.424, toward the rarer class 2, so the common class 1 gets more room.
